title: Triggers, audit trails, and hidden side effects
summary: Trace row and statement triggers, old/new values, multirow updates, and rollback.
intro: A trigger is invoked by a declared database event rather than an explicit caller command. It is powerful precisely because it runs on paths that an application author might not see in the submitted SQL.
outcomes: Specify event, timing, granularity, condition, and action.
Build a NULL-aware mark audit for more than one updated row.
Explain transactional side effects, recursion, and when a constraint is better.

sections.title: 1. The trigger contract has five parts
paragraphs: State the event (such as UPDATE), timing (BEFORE, AFTER, or an applicable INSTEAD OF), granularity (row or statement), condition, and action. A row trigger runs for each qualifying row. A statement trigger runs for the statement and may receive sets of changed rows through product-specific mechanisms.

An UPDATE affecting zero rows still has statement-level consequences in engines that support statement triggers, while no row trigger has a changed row to process. AFTER describes timing within database execution; it does not generally mean after the transaction commits.
sections.alt: One UPDATE matches two enrolments. Row-trigger engines invoke the audit action twice; SQL Server receives inserted and deleted sets and performs a set-based audit insert. Commit preserves both base and audit changes; rollback undoes both.
sections.caption: Trigger actions participate in the transaction in this design. A two-row update must produce two audit rows, not one arbitrary row.

sections.title: 2. Build a visible, NULL-aware audit
paragraphs: This scratch example records old and new marks. The demo UPDATE changes Asha from 82 to 83 and Ravi from 88 to 89. It does not change Mira's NULL mark. A trigger must test an actual value change, not only whether mark appears in the UPDATE column list.

postgresql.note: Run once in a fresh Unit 3 fixture. This exercise modifies two marks; restore the fixture before unrelated exercises. The trigger body does not commit.

oracle.note: Oracle 19c row trigger: :OLD and :NEW refer to values of the changed row. Slash submits the trigger definition in a script.

mysql.note: MySQL row trigger: <=> is NULL-safe equality; NOT detects an actual change. Use InnoDB for transactional base and audit tables.

mariadb.note: MariaDB row trigger: <=> handles transitions to and from NULL. Use InnoDB transactional tables.

sqlite.note: SQLite row trigger: IS NOT detects a change including NULL transitions. Changes to the audit table roll back with the triggering transaction.

sqlserver.note: SQL Server statement trigger: inserted/deleted can contain many rows. This exercise changes marks only; the composite identity remains unchanged. GO separates client batches.

sections.title: 3. NULL-aware comparison and multirow correctness
paragraphs: OLD.mark <> NEW.mark alone misses a change from NULL to 70 or from 70 to NULL because the comparison is UNKNOWN. PostgreSQL IS DISTINCT FROM, MySQL/MariaDB NULL-safe equality, SQLite IS NOT, and explicit Oracle/SQL Server predicates express the intended distinction.

SQL Server triggers process inserted and deleted rowsets. Assigning a scalar variable from inserted and assuming one row would silently mishandle a multirow statement. The sample joins old/new sets on the unchanged composite identity; mutable identity would require a stable matching design or a different operation policy.

sections.title: 4. Rollback, failure, and scope
paragraphs: For this transactional audit design, a rollback undoes both the base mark change and its audit insert. Test it by starting a transaction after creating the trigger, changing a mark, observing the audit row, then rolling back and rechecking both tables. Oracle DDL implicit commits mean trigger creation must be outside the rollback exercise.

A failed trigger action can fail the triggering statement. It should not silently swallow an audit write error if the requirement is that every accepted change be audited. External emails and HTTP calls are not automatically rolled back with database rows; use an appropriate transactional outbox or other explicit integration design when needed.

sections.title: 5. Prefer visible rules and control trigger interactions
paragraphs: Use constraints for ordinary key, reference, required-value, and row-domain rules. Triggers are reasonable for carefully designed audit or derived-side-effect requirements. They can also create recursion, hidden latency, unexpected lock ordering, or dependency chains.

Oracle row triggers can encounter mutating-table restrictions when querying or changing their triggering table. Do not repair that by committing inside the trigger. Other engines have their own recursion and table-access restrictions. A trigger that counts enrolments without concurrency control is not automatically a safe course-capacity constraint.

sections.title: 6. Boundary exercises
paragraphs: Run an UPDATE setting mark to its existing value: no audit row should be added. Change Mira's DB101 mark from NULL to 70: exactly one audit row should appear with old_mark NULL. Then change it back to NULL and check the reverse transition. Run one statement changing two non-NULL marks and verify two rows.

These tests distinguish a real value-change audit from a statement-column detector. They also reveal single-row assumptions and bad NULL comparisons that a simple one-row numeric update would never expose.

revision: Trace a two-row update and NULL transitions.
Explain rollback and prefer constraints for declarative invariants.

questions.question: Does AFTER UPDATE mean the trigger runs after COMMIT?
answer: No. In this design it runs during execution of the data-changing statement, before the enclosing transaction is committed. Its audit writes are transactional and are undone on rollback.

questions.question: Why is OLD.mark <> NEW.mark insufficient?
answer: A comparison involving NULL is UNKNOWN. It misses transitions between missing and recorded values. Use the selected DBMS's NULL-aware comparison or the explicit transition predicates.

questions.question: What is wrong with reading one scalar value from SQL Server inserted?
answer: A statement trigger can receive many inserted rows. Picking one cannot audit every changed row and may be nondeterministic. Write a set-based operation over inserted/deleted and a valid stable matching key.

questions.question: Can a rolled-back change remain in this audit table?
answer: Not when both the base and audit changes participate in the same ordinary transaction as shown. A durable record of failed attempts would require a deliberately different design and failure/security analysis, not a hidden commit in this trigger.
